name: Jjak-mat-chu-gi
description: Jjak-mat-chu-gi (짝맞추기 - 'Making Pairs') is a traditional Korean domino game played with Gol-pae (bone tiles). Unlike Western dominoes where players match end-to-end, this is a 'pair-making' game where the objective is to form specific combinations (Civil and Military pairs). It is a draw-and-discard game similar in structure to Rummy but played with tiles.

overview.description: Jjak-mat-chu-gi (짝맞추기 - 'Making Pairs') is a traditional Korean domino game played with Gol-pae (bone tiles). Unlike Western dominoes where players match end-to-end, this is a 'pair-making' game where the objective is to form specific combinations (Civil and Military pairs). It is a draw-and-discard game similar in structure to Rummy but played with tiles.

history.origins: Dates back centuries in Korea, adapted from Chinese domino sets. It was first documented in Western literature by Stewart Culin in 1895 in his book 'Korean Games'.
timeline: 1800s: Traditional social game for Korean scholars and elders.
Present: Played mostly by enthusiasts and elders; a precursor to modern Korean card games like Go-Stop.
history.cultural: Used as both a social pastime and a tool for gambling (Seotda-style).
history.evolution: The game's suit system (Civil vs. Military) reflects the historical social structure of the Joseon dynasty.

setup.deck: 32 tiles: 11 'Civil' pairs (matching) and 10 'Military' tiles (unique, paired by total spots).
setup.dealing: First player draws 6 tiles, others 5 each. Remaining tiles form a face-down reserve. First player is chosen by draw (tile 2-5 or highest spots plays first).

rules.objective: Be the first to form three complete pairs in your hand.
rules.gameplay:
1. Players draw a tile from the reserve and discard one into the center.
2. A player can 'chow' (claim) an opponent's discard ONLY if it completes a pair.
3. Pairs are laid face-down until the hand is won.
keyRules: Each turn: either claim the previous player's discard to complete a pair, or draw one from the reserve.
After acquiring a tile, lay down any completed pairs face down, then discard one tile face up.
First to complete three pairs wins. With 2 or 3 players, 6-6 cannot be the third pair; with 4 players it can.

strategy.basic: Prioritize Civil pairs early as they are easier to recognize. Keep the Supreme pair (tiles 1-2 and 2-4) if you find them—they are rare and valuable.
strategy.intermediate: Efficiency: If you have a Military tile like 6-1, keep an eye out for its counterparts 5-2 or 4-3. Knowing the pip totals is essential for speed.
strategy.advanced: Discard Management: Watch what tiles others are discarding. If both 1-1 tiles have been discarded, any remaining single 1-1 is a dead tile and should be discarded immediately.
tips: Memorize the Military pairs (7s, 8s, 9s) to quickly identify matches.
The Supreme pair (4-2 and 2-1) is the only pair that is neither identical nor shares a total.

variations.name: Win only by reserve
variations.description: A player's third (winning) pair can only be made by matching a tile drawn from the reserve; winning by taking a discard is not allowed.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Source describes rule change only; no engine overrides documented yet.

variations.name: Row draw
variations.description: Shuffled tiles are placed in a row; tiles are drawn from one end of the row instead of a reserve pile.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Layout variant described in source; no engine overrides specified.

variations.name: Alternative military pairing
variations.description: Some sources use a different grouping for Military pairs: e.g. 2-6 with 3-6, 2-5 with 3-5, 2-4 with 3-4, 1-4 with 2-3, 1-2 with 4-5.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Alternative pairing from Culin; could add meld overrides when implementing.
